Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 5 of 10): Free Trade, Opium and Abolition, 1815–1856

Summary: After Waterloo, Britain had no serious naval rival for nearly a century. It used that position to abolish slavery in its colonies, force opium on China, annex the Punjab and much of Burma, and send settlers to Australia, New Zealand, Canada and southern Africa. This post covers 1815 to 1856, including the Baptist War in Jamaica, the Canadian rebellions, the retreat from Kabul, the Irish Famine and the Taiping Rebellion.

---

## The big picture

This was the age of the "Pax Britannica", which was peaceful mainly from London's point of view. Britain fought only one war against a European power (Crimea), but its forces were fighting somewhere in Asia, Africa or the Pacific almost every year.

Three trends overlapped:

- **Abolition and its limits.** Slavery in most British colonies ended in 1834, but enslavers, not the enslaved, were compensated, and a new system of Indian indentured labour quickly took its place.
- **Free trade and "informal empire".** Britain often preferred to open markets by treaty or gunboat rather than to rule directly. The Opium Wars are the clearest example.
- **Settler colonies.** Large-scale emigration to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the Cape created societies that would later govern themselves, at heavy cost to Indigenous peoples.

## Main timeline (1815–1838)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1816 | **Bussa's Rebellion**, Barbados | Largest slave revolt in Barbados's history |
| 1817–1818 | Third Anglo-Maratha War | The Peshwa is deposed; the Company becomes the dominant power in India |
| 1817–1818 | Uva Rebellion in Ceylon | Suppressed with a scorched-earth campaign |
| 1819 | Stamford Raffles founds a British post at **Singapore**; Peterloo Massacre in Manchester | |
| 1823 | **Demerara rebellion** (British Guiana); Anti-Slavery Society founded | About 10,000 enslaved people rise; hundreds killed; the missionary John Smith dies in prison, which outrages British public opinion |
| 1824–1826 | First Anglo-Burmese War | Britain takes Assam, Arakan and Tenasserim. One of the most expensive Company wars |
| 1824 | Anglo-Dutch Treaty divides the Malay world; Britain gets Malacca | The line still roughly separates Malaysia and Indonesia |
| c.1824–1831 | **Black War** in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) | Martial law; the Aboriginal population of Tasmania is devastated |
| 1826 | Straits Settlements (Penang, Malacca, Singapore) formed | |
| 1829 | Sati abolished in Bengal; Catholic Emancipation in the UK; Swan River colony (Western Australia) | |
| 1831–1832 | **Baptist War** in Jamaica, led by Samuel Sharpe | Up to 60,000 people take part; over 300 executed, including Sharpe. Speeds up abolition |
| 1833 | **Slavery Abolition Act** | In force on 1 August 1834; about 800,000 people freed in principle; £20 million compensation paid to slave owners |
| 1834–1838 | "Apprenticeship" forces the formerly enslaved to keep working unpaid for most of the week | Ended early, in 1838, after protest |
| 1834 | Indian indentured labour to Mauritius begins | Over the following 80 years, more than a million Indians are shipped to plantations across the empire |
| 1835 | Macaulay's "Minute on Education"; the Great Trek of Boer settlers away from British rule begins | English-language education policy in India |
| 1836 | South Australia founded | |
| 1837 | **Victoria becomes queen**; rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada | |
| 1838 | Durham Report commissioned (published 1839) | Recommends "responsible government" for Canada, the model for later dominions |

## Main timeline (1839–1856)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1839 | Aden taken; Lin Zexu destroys British opium at Canton | |
| 1839–1842 | **First Opium War** | Treaty of Nanking (1842): Hong Kong ceded, five ports opened, an indemnity paid. The first "unequal treaty" |
| 1839–1842 | **First Anglo-Afghan War** | Retreat from Kabul in January 1842: an army of about 4,500 soldiers and 12,000 followers is destroyed |
| 1840 | **Treaty of Waitangi** (6 February); Act of Union joins Upper and Lower Canada | The English and Māori versions of Waitangi differ on sovereignty, a dispute still central in New Zealand |
| 1843 | Sindh conquered; Natal annexed | |
| 1845–1846 | First Anglo-Sikh War; Flagstaff War (Northern War) in New Zealand | Sikh empire was weakened after Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 |
| 1845–1852 | **Great Irish Famine** | About one million die and around a million emigrate; food exports from Ireland continued |
| 1846 | Repeal of the Corn Laws | Britain commits to free trade |
| 1848 | Young Irelander rising; responsible government in Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada | |
| 1848–1849 | Second Anglo-Sikh War | **Punjab annexed (1849)**; the Koh-i-Noor sent to Queen Victoria |
| 1848–1856 | Lord Dalhousie's "Doctrine of Lapse" | States without a natural male heir are annexed (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and others) |
| 1851 | Gold rushes in New South Wales and Victoria; Great Exhibition in London | |
| 1852 | Second Anglo-Burmese War | Lower Burma annexed |
| 1853 | First passenger railway in India (Bombay to Thane) | |
| 1853–1856 | **Crimean War** with France and the Ottomans against Russia | Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole |
| 1854 | **Eureka Stockade** at Ballarat | Gold miners rebel over licences and representation |
| 1855–1856 | **Santal Hul** (Santhal rebellion) | Thousands of Santals killed |
| 1856 | Annexation of Awadh (Oudh) | A major grievance before 1857 |
| 1856 | Second Opium War (Arrow War) begins | |

| 1846–1848 | Mexican–American War | North America |
| 1848 | **Revolutions across Europe**; *The Communist Manifesto* | Europe, the same year as the Young Irelander rising |
| 1850–1864 | **Taiping Rebellion**, the deadliest civil war of the 19th century | China |

## Resistance: wars, risings and rebellions

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1816 | Bussa's Rebellion | Barbados | Suppressed; about 120 killed in fighting and over 140 executed (figures vary) |
| 1817–1818 | Uva Rebellion | Ceylon | Crushed |
| 1817 | Paika Rebellion | Odisha (Orissa) | Suppressed |
| 1823 | Demerara rebellion | British Guiana | Suppressed |
| 1824 | Kittur rising under Rani Chennamma | Karnataka | Crushed; she died in captivity |
| 1831–1832 | Baptist War | Jamaica | Suppressed; accelerated the Abolition Act |
| 1834–1836, 1846–1847, 1850–1853 | Cape Frontier (Xhosa) Wars | Eastern Cape | Xhosa land gradually annexed |
| 1837–1838 | Rebellions in Lower Canada (Papineau) and Upper Canada (Mackenzie) | Canada | Defeated, but led to the Durham Report |
| 1839–1842 | Afghan resistance under Akbar Khan | Afghanistan | British withdrawal |
| 1845–1849 | Sikh Empire | Punjab | Annexed |
| 1845–1872 | New Zealand Wars begin with the Flagstaff War (Hone Heke) | New Zealand | Continued in the 1860s |
| 1854 | Eureka Stockade | Victoria (Australia) | Crushed in 15 minutes, but most miners' demands were met within a year |
| 1855–1856 | Santal Hul, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu | Bengal Presidency | Brutally put down |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1833–1834.** Britain ended slavery in its colonies and began shipping Indian indentured labourers to Mauritius in practically the same year. Critics at the time called indenture "a new system of slavery".
- **1839–1842.** Britain was fighting the First Opium War and the First Afghan War at the same time, and the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in the middle. The army destroyed in the retreat from Kabul and the forces that won at Nanking were both largely funded from Indian revenues.
- **1845–1849.** The Great Irish Famine, the two Anglo-Sikh Wars, and the start of the New Zealand Wars overlapped. In the same years Britain repealed the Corn Laws and Europe went through the revolutions of 1848.
- **1850–1856.** China's Taiping Rebellion was killing millions while Britain fought Russia in Crimea and prepared the Second Opium War against the same Qing government.
- **2015.** The UK government only finished repaying the loan that financed the 1834 slavery compensation in 2015, a fact that went viral after the Treasury mentioned it in 2018.

## Sources and flags

- Catherine Hall and others, *Legacies of British Slave-ownership* (2014), and the UCL database: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs
- Julia Lovell, *The Opium War: Drugs, Dreams and the Making of China* (2011).
- William Dalrymple, *Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan* (2013).
- Claudia Orange, *The Treaty of Waitangi* (1987); New Zealand History site: https://nzhistory.govt.nz
- Cecil Woodham-Smith, *The Great Hunger* (1962).
- Hugh Tinker, *A New System of Slavery: The Export of Indian Labour Overseas 1830–1920* (1974).
- Henry Reynolds, *The Other Side of the Frontier* (1981), on Australian frontier violence.
- **Flag:** Numbers in the Kabul retreat, the Baptist War and Bussa's Rebellion are commonly cited estimates. The Irish Famine figures (about one million deaths) are the standard estimate; the true number is uncertain. The 2015 loan repayment fact refers to the gilts that financed the compensation; it was confirmed by HM Treasury in 2018, though the way it was framed caused some debate.
